paragraphs.heading: What it is
paragraphs.text: Transcription is the step in which a cell copies a stretch of DNA into RNA so that a gene can be expressed. Some of the RNA made this way is messenger RNA (mRNA), which can code for proteins. Other stretches become non-coding RNA. DNA and RNA are both nucleic acids, built from chains of nucleotides.

paragraphs.heading: Reading one strand
paragraphs.text: An enzyme called RNA polymerase reads the DNA and builds a matching RNA strand, the primary transcript. It uses only one of the two DNA strands as its template, reading it from the 3' end toward the 5' end. The RNA grows the other way, 5' to 3', because the polymerase can add new nucleotides only at the 3' end. The finished RNA matches the other DNA strand, called the coding strand, except that RNA has uracil (U) wherever DNA has thymine (T). By convention, DNA sequences are written out using this coding strand.

paragraphs.heading: Not the same as copying DNA
paragraphs.text: Transcription differs from DNA replication in several ways. Because only one strand is read, in one direction, it needs neither the Okazaki fragments seen in DNA replication nor an RNA primer to get started. It also has fewer and weaker proofreading checks. So its copies are less faithful than those made when DNA is replicated.

paragraphs.heading: Parts of a gene
paragraphs.text: A stretch of DNA that codes for a protein can hold a coding sequence, which is turned into the protein, and regulatory sequences, which steer and control making it. The regulatory part before the coding sequence is the 5' untranslated region (5'UTR), and the part after it is the 3'UTR. Transcription itself runs in four stages: initiation, promoter escape, elongation and termination.

paragraphs.heading: Switches near and far
paragraphs.text: In mammals, getting transcription started is controlled by many regulatory DNA elements. Some, like the core promoter, sit near the spot where transcription begins; a core promoter plus general transcription factors can start transcription, but usually only at a low level. Others lie far away, including enhancers, silencers and insulators. Enhancers, with the transcription factors bound to them, play a leading part, and an activated enhancer can raise a gene's transcription as much as 100-fold.

paragraphs.heading: Looping the DNA
paragraphs.text: Enhancers usually work by looping the DNA so they come physically close to the promoter of the gene they control, sometimes across tens or hundreds of thousands of nucleotides. In one study of brain cortical neurons, researchers found 24,937 such loops. A pair of connector proteins, such as CTCF, holds each loop in place, one anchored on the enhancer and one on the promoter. A protein complex called Mediator then passes signals from the enhancer's transcription factors straight to RNA polymerase II sitting on the promoter.

paragraphs.heading: Chemical tags
paragraphs.text: Another layer of control is chemical. At about 60% of promoters, transcription is also regulated by methylation of cytosines at CpG sites, where a cytosine is followed by a guanine. The human genome has about 28 million of these sites, and in most mammal tissues 70% to 80% of their cytosines are methylated. Active promoters, however, often carry clusters of unmethylated sites called CpG islands.
